title: Edge scheduler preemption spike investigation notes
content:
Summary:
We observed a cluster-wide spike in scheduler preemptions and pod churn in the edge (us-west1-edge) cluster between 2025-02-11T23:42:00Z and 2025-02-12T00:30:00Z. Visible symptoms: sudden increase in pod evictions, ~30% of pods in edge pool restarted at least once, and a correlated increase in etcd write latency and API-server 5xx errors for ~40 minutes. Impact: customer-facing low-latency endpoints experienced tail latency > 2s and a small fraction (~0.6%) of requests dropped due to backend 500s. No data loss or long-term outages, but degraded SLAs for the window.

Initial hypothesis (v1):
- A wave of spot/discount node reclaims (cloud provider preemption) triggered aggressive cluster-autoscaler (CA) reactions.
- CA scaled up on-demand pool but did so with short delay, causing scheduler to reorder work and preempt lower-priority pods to make room for high-priority ones; combined with many small preemptions this caused scheduling thrash and increased API-server load.
- PodPriority values and PodDisruptionBudgets (PDBs) were not aligned for the most-churned workloads, allowing many preemptions simultaneously.

What we saw (data points):
- Eviction rate: baseline ~0.2 evictions/min -> peaked ~26 evictions/min at 2025-02-11T23:48Z.
- Scheduler scheduling latency p95: baseline 120ms -> peaked 1.8s.
- etcd apply latency p95: baseline 7ms -> peaked 120ms.
- API server 500 rate: 0.03% -> peaked 1.2% of requests.
- Cloud provider event logs: multiple spot termination notices for nodes in edge-spot-pool around 23:40-23:46Z (IDs: gke-edge-s-*-usw1).

Key timeline (collected from monitoring + oncall notes):
- 23:37 UTC: First spot termination notice in provider logs.
- 23:40 UTC: CA sees capacity reduction; starts scale-up attempts into on-demand pool. CA log: "scale-up: need 18 nodes, finding best nodegroup".
- 23:44 UTC: Evictions start climbing; kube-scheduler preemption events recorded in system logs.
- 23:48 UTC: Eviction spike peak. Several controllers (ingress, sidecars) create new pods; scheduler attempts to satisfy priorities, preempting multiple low-priority pods across nodes.
- 23:50 UTC: API server 5xx rate climbs as controllers and nodes flood etcd with updates.
- 00:02 UTC: Mitigation: oncall ran emergency action: increased on-demand pool min nodes from 8 -> 12 (manual override), cordoned 3 most unstable nodes to reduce churn.
- 00:15 UTC: Evictions rate drops; scheduler latency returns toward baseline by 00:28 UTC.
- 00:30 UTC: System stable; follow-ups started.

Evidence snippets (selected):
- Example scheduler event: "Preempting pod frontend-low-1234 to make room for backend-high-9876 (priority 1000 > 500)"
- kubectl get pods --field-selector=status.phase!=Running --namespace=prod-edge (snippet during peak):
  frontend-low-1234  Evicted   23:47:12  Node gke-edge-s-23
  metrics-agent-5x   Evicted   23:47:20  Node gke-edge-s-12
- CA log excerpt: "will not scale up: limited by quota in zone us-west1-a" (this delayed >30s for some requests)

Immediate mitigations applied: (actions we took during the incident)
- Manually increased on-demand pool to absorb incoming pods (oncall: cordon->drain not used broadly to avoid extra evictions). Owner: Miguel.
- Temporarily relaxed CA scale-down aggressiveness (to avoid removing on-demand nodes quickly).
- Applied a short-term override to PDB enforcement for low-priority batch jobs (migrated via kubeclient to reduce simultaneous eviction targets).
- Raised alert threshold for preemption rate so SRE gets earlier signal next time.

Root-cause analysis (working):
1) Primary driver: Spot node reclaim wave in edge-spot-pool. Provider returned many preemption notices in a short window.
2) Secondary driver: CA configuration and node pool quotas caused delayed and batched scale-up decisions (CA had to evaluate quota/limits leading to retries). This made pressure last longer and increased eviction churn.
3) Contributing factors: a) PodPriority distribution: a number of mid-priority stateful controllers exist that are easily preemptible; b) PDBs did not cover enough of critical services so multiple critical-replaceable pods were evicted simultaneously; c) Some nodes were eligible for preemption and for draining by daemonset controllers causing extra churn; d) Cluster lacked a throttling mechanism for preemption-induced API churn (i.e., many controllers reconciling at once).

Why this is different from a normal node-pressure event:
- Node-pressure / OOM events usually show resource exhaustion on nodes that is slower and limited to specific nodes. This event was driven externally (provider reclaim) and caused many small, fast evictions across many nodes, which interacts badly with CA heuristics and scheduler preemption logic.

Runbook gaps we identified:
- No documented escalation path for "spot reclaim wave" as a first-class event. Runbooks have OOM/pressure and CNI, but not preemption surge guidance.
- CA configs lack explicit guardrails for sudden multi-node spot loss (e.g., conservative minimum on-demand buffer size per zone).
- No automation to temporarily throttle controller reconcilers or pace PDB updates during spikes.

Proposed follow-ups & action items (owners + ETA):
- SRE-1422: Add a preemption-surge play to SRE runbook (doc) with exactly these mitigations: temporarily increase on-demand min pool, cordon candidates, and adjust CA flags (owner: Aisha, ETA: 2025-02-21).
- infra-ops-67: Change CA config: ensure per-zone on-demand buffer of 2 nodes for edge clusters by default (owner: Miguel, ETA: 2025-03-01).
- sched-65: Review PodPriority tiers and reclassify middle-priority batch jobs as lower priority where acceptable; create stable priority for latency-sensitive services (owner: Priya, ETA: 2025-02-28).
- pdb-31: Audit existing PDBs for critical services in edge clusters; ensure we don't allow simultaneous eviction of more than 20% of replicas (owner: Noah, ETA: 2025-02-25).
- metrics-90: Add a new metric and alert: preemption_rate (evictions initiated by preemption) > 5/min for 5m -> page SRE on-call (owner: monitoring, ETA: 2025-02-18).
- autoscaler-ops-12: Add a CA health-check that detects quota-limited scale-up loops and surfaces an alert to owners instead of silently retrying (owner: infra, ETA: 2025-03-10).

Runbook draft (short) — to be added to ops playbooks: (this is a working checklist for preemption surge)
- Step 0: Detect: preemption_rate > 5/min OR spot-termination webhook shows > 10 nodes flagged within 5m.
- Step 1: Assess scope: list affected nodegroups (gcloud/az/eks). tag affected zone.
- Step 2: Quick mitigation: if on-demand buffer < threshold, manually increase on-demand pool min by +N (N = max(2, floor(spot-lost/3))).
- Step 3: Cordons: cordon the most unstable nodes (by termination age) but avoid mass drains to prevent cascading evictions.
- Step 4: CA tuning: disable aggressive scale-down and check quota failures; if CA logs show quota errors, open infra incident with cloudops.
- Step 5: Stabilize: reduce controller concurrency where safe (helm/patch deployment replicas-> 0? Not generally advised; prefer throttling via annotations if controllers support it).
- Step 6: Postmortem: capture full CA logs + provider termination notices; reopen for root cause follow-up.

Quick checks & commands used during the incident (notes to self):
- kubectl get nodes -o wide --selector=pool=edge-spot
- kubectl get events --all-namespaces --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail -n 200 | grep Preempt
- gcloud compute instances describe <node-id> --zone=us-west1-a | grep termination
- kubectl -n kube-system logs deployment/cluster-autoscaler | sed -n '1,200p'
- kubectl get pdb --all-namespaces -o wide | grep edge

Open questions / unresolved items:
- Why did CA choose to request such a large number of nodes at once? (suspicion: CA saw pending pods with high resource requests; need to inspect pod resource requests and CA scale-up algorithm logs).
- Could we have reduced API-server write amplification by queuing certificate/controller writes differently? (need deeper analysis into controller reconcile storms).

Notes to reviewers:
- This doc is intentionally informal; preserve the timeline and raw snippets. When we convert to the full postmortem, we should add graphs (evictions/min, scheduler latency, etcd latency) and attach CA logs and provider termination list.
- We should also consider a short-term policy: avoid >40% of edge capacity being spot-backed for business-critical clusters until CA per-zone buffer is implemented.

Misc/learning:
- Preemption spikes are a distinct failure mode from simple node pressure — they create a cascade by forcing scheduler to mediate resource conflicts quickly across the control plane. Planning and automation should treat 'reclaim wave' as an explicit threat model.

TODO (assigned):
- Aisha: Draft runbook entry and notify kube-scheduling working group (ETA 2025-02-21).
- Miguel: Push CA min buffer change to staging, run load test (ETA 2025-02-25).
- Priya: Audit priorities for edge namespaces and propose remappings (ETA 2025-02-28).
- Noah: PDB audit and quick fixes for critical services (ETA 2025-02-25).

End of notes.

- "23:50:33 - miguel: manual on-demand bump applied (min 8->12), cordoned nodes: gke-edge-s-12,gke-edge-s-23,gke-edge-s-30"
- "00:05:02 - system cooling; evictions down to 3/min"
